analysis.investment_thesis: Ashwini Container Movers offers a P/E of 13.60 that superficially passes my threshold, but a ROE of 0.72% reveals earnings so thin they offer no real return on the underlying assets. With no balance sheet data to verify margin of safety, this is speculation dressed as value.
key_strengths: P/E of 13.60 narrowly satisfies my <15 requirement
High promoter holding of 66.67% suggests skin in the game
FII/DII combined at 14.57% indicates some institutional scrutiny
key_risks: ROE of 0.72% is near-zero — the business earns almost nothing on shareholders' capital
Road transport is a commoditized, low-barrier industry with no discernible moat
Critical Graham metrics (P/B, current ratio, D/E, dividend history) are unavailable — cannot confirm margin of safety
red_flags: ROE of 0.72% fails any reasonable profitability test — I demand businesses that demonstrate earning power
No balance sheet data provided — cannot calculate Graham Number or assess solvency
Small regional operator (Maharashtra/Gujarat only) with INR 208 Cr market cap — illiquid and operationally fragile
No dividend history mentioned — no evidence of real cash returns to shareholders
analysis.detailed_analysis:
A P/E of 13.60 catches the eye, but it is a hollow figure when ROE stands at a mere 0.72%. That means for every 100 rupees of shareholders' equity, this company generates less than 1 rupee of profit. The Graham Number requires both earnings and book value to yield a fair price; with such feeble earning power, the Graham Number would be negligible regardless of book value. Incorporated only in 2012, this company also lacks the long earnings track record — ideally 5–10 years of uninterrupted profits — that I require before committing capital.

Road transport in India is a brutally competitive, low-margin commodity business. Ashwini operates regionally, confined largely to Maharashtra and Gujarat, giving it no geographic scale and no pricing power. The absence of P/B ratio, current ratio, debt-to-equity, and dividend history means I cannot complete even my basic checklist. Mr. Market may occasionally offer genuine bargains, but a business that earns practically nothing on its equity is not a bargain at any price — it is a slow drain on capital. I require a significant margin of safety, and here I cannot even determine what is safe.
